passage:
Paragraph A
The islands of the Pacific are separated by distances that would be considered serious even by a modern yacht, and many of them are low, small and invisible until a vessel is almost upon them. They were nonetheless settled, deliberately and repeatedly, by people sailing double-hulled canoes with no compass, no chart and no instrument of any kind. For most of the twentieth century the standard explanation was that this had happened by accident — canoes blown off course, carried by currents, arriving by luck. The explanation had the advantage of requiring nothing to be explained.

Paragraph B
It was undermined, awkwardly, by the winds themselves. The prevailing trade winds in the region blow from the east, which means that the great movement of settlement, which ran from west to east, was a movement against them. A vessel blown off course travels downwind, and downwind was the wrong way. Sailing east meant beating into the wind on purpose, and doing so with enough confidence to carry the food, water, plants and animals needed to found a settlement at the other end. Accidental drift could not account for the direction of travel.

Paragraph C
What the navigators used instead was a system that had to be carried entirely in the head. Its foundation was the stars. Particular stars rise and set at fixed points on the horizon, and a navigator memorised long sequences of them: as one star climbed too high to be useful, the next in the sequence rose in the same place and the canoe was steered by that. A route was learnt as a series of such stars, in order, together with the equivalent series for the return. In daylight, when no stars were visible, the swells took over — the long regular waves generated by distant weather systems, which hold their direction for days and can be read by the motion of the hull as reliably as by the eye.

Paragraph D
The most striking element was a mental technique for keeping track of position. The navigator held in mind a reference island, off to one side of the route and often out of sight, and imagined it moving backwards past the canoe as the voyage progressed, checked against the star sequence. The canoe was treated as stationary and the world as sliding past it. To a modern reader accustomed to plotting a moving vessel on a fixed chart, this sounds like a needless inversion. Its practical value is that it requires no paper: the navigator can state at any moment how far along the journey he is by naming what lies abeam of him.

Paragraph E
Finding the island at the end remained the hardest part, because a low atoll is visible from perhaps ten miles and an error of ten miles over a voyage of a thousand is very small indeed. The answer was to stop aiming at the island. Navigators learnt the signs that surround land and effectively widened the target: certain seabirds fly out to fish at dawn and return at dusk, so their evening direction points to land; a stationary cloud may sit above a peak, and the pale-green underside of a cloud can betray a lagoon below; drifting vegetation and particular patterns of swell reflected from an unseen shore all extend the zone in which land can be detected. A group of islands could in this way present a target eighty or a hundred miles wide.

Paragraph F
By the middle of the last century very few people still held the whole system. It had been transmitted orally, over years of apprenticeship, and it did not survive the arrival of engines and charts in most of the region. It persisted mainly in parts of Micronesia, where a small number of navigators had trained in the traditional way and continued to make ocean passages, and it was from that thin surviving thread that the knowledge was recovered.

Paragraph G
The decisive test came in 1976, when a replica double-hulled canoe sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti guided by a navigator from the Caroline Islands, carrying no instruments and taking no readings. The distance was well over two thousand miles and the course lay across the trade winds. The canoe arrived. The voyage did not prove how the original settlement had been carried out, since a modern crew could not recover a lost tradition merely by imitating it, but it disposed of the claim that such a passage was impossible without instruments, and that claim had been doing most of the work in the accidental-drift argument.

Paragraph H
What followed was less a scholarly correction than a revival. Canoes were built across the Pacific, apprentices were trained, and voyages were made between island groups that had not exchanged a sailing canoe in generations. Academically the question of how the Pacific was settled is now approached mainly through genetics, linguistics and the dating of settlement sites. But the navigation itself has ceased to be a historical puzzle and has become a living practice again, which is not the usual fate of a lost technique.

(Glossary: swell: long regular waves produced by distant weather rather than by local wind; atoll: a low ring-shaped coral island; abeam: at right angles to the side of a vessel; apprenticeship: a long period of training under an expert.)
